chapter: Reflections on Paris guitarists and saxophonists
title: How Hawkins and Benny Carter make complexity sound natural
summary: Replying to Crouch about Hawkins's early harmonic ideas, Butler says great musicians absorb foundations until the result sounds easy, as Benny Carter's humble mastery does.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Well, do you think it was because you know, because, you know, there's some early work of his even, like in the early '30's where he was dealing with a whole tone --

But you didn't realize it because he was playing music from great music. You see, when a band plays some (inaudible) music -- it runs all together and becomes a natural thing. You understand. That's what happened.

You see, for example, you don't realize for a man -- Polybrook (phonetic), well, this man is speaking, he would talk to you in Spanish, French and German and everything and you don't realize it, realize what he's doing.
In fact, he don't realize it and you say -- he was
something else --but he has gotten the foundation and he's been doing it, so it's nothing for him and he modifies it, and makes it look like it's nothing. That's what he did.

Now, Benny Carter, you see, Benny Carter, when he plays, it sounds like nothing but if you listen to what that man is doing and -- (inaudible) -- piano, and so he come from there. That's what happens, see. That's what happens to you, so that's what he does.

These -- what do you call -- (sentence in foreign language) -- that means, that man, he knows everything. But he's humble with it. He doesn't exploit it. He's not arrogant. He's got mother-wit, he's an artist and everything, but he doesn't exploit it.
Like the man who is arrogant -- why, yes, I've got -- this other man, he's got horsesense, he keeps quiet.
